t: 3456. Find Special Substring of Length K
o: We need a maximal-looking block of exactly k identical characters whose immediate neighbors (if any) differ. In "aaabaaa" with k = 3, the second "aaa" qualifies because it is preceded by 'b' and ends the string. Scanning runs of equal characters answers this directly: a run of length exactly k with differing neighbors is precisely the target.
k: Decompose the string into maximal runs of equal characters.
A run qualifies iff its length equals k, the char before it differs (or it starts the string), and the char after it differs (or it ends the string).

a.i: Try each index i as the start of the special substring: verify s[i..i+k-1] are all equal and the neighbors differ. Simple O(n·k), perfectly fine for n ≤ 100.
s: For each i from 0 to n-k: check all k characters equal.
If yes, check s[i-1] (if exists) ≠ s[i] and s[i+k] (if exists) ≠ s[i].
Return true on the first success, false otherwise.
a.t: O(n·k) — each start scans up to k characters

a.i: Group the string into maximal runs of identical characters in one pass. Only a run whose length is exactly k can qualify, and its neighbors automatically differ (they bound a maximal run), so the check reduces to comparing run length with k.
s: Walk i through the string, extending j while s[j] == s[i].
If j - i == k and the boundary conditions hold, return true.
Jump i to j and repeat; return false at the end.

w: The run-length view is the cleanest explanation: 'maximal run of length exactly k'. Pitfall: a run longer than k does NOT contain a valid substring, because any length-k piece inside it touches an equal neighbor — this is why checking every start naively still needs the neighbor conditions. Edge cases: k = n (whole string must be one run), k = 1 (any isolated character works). Follow-up: return the count of special substrings instead — same run scan, counting matches.
